summary: Organizations can now invite people. A Product invites an email with a role, gets a one-time token, sends it however it likes, and later accepts it for a signed-in user, which creates the membership.

verdict.ask: A new invitation resource: status is computed rather than stored, a row lock keeps one pending invitation per email, and the token alone is enough to join.
verdict.doorNote: Additive only: one new table, eight new routes, four new event types. Nothing that exists changes shape, and the down migration drops the table. It becomes one-way once a Product builds on the contract.

decisions.title: Status is computed on read, never stored
decisions.choice: No `status` column. Pending means `accepted_at` is null and `expires_at` is in the future. Expired is only ever computed.
decisions.why: Invitations expire when the clock passes, so there is no job flipping rows and no stale status to drift.
decisions.instead: A stored status plus a scheduled job that marks rows expired.
decisions.cost: "One pending per email" depends on `now()`, so it cannot be a partial unique index. The service has to enforce it.

decisions.title: An organization row lock keeps one pending invitation per email
decisions.choice: Every write first takes `SELECT … FOR NO KEY UPDATE` on the organization, then checks for a pending invitation and for a member with that email.
decisions.why: Two concurrent creates for the same email queue on the lock, so only one can pass the check. A CT runs the race.
decisions.instead: A partial unique index (impossible here) or SERIALIZABLE isolation with retries.
decisions.cost: All invitation writes in one organization run one at a time, and they wait on any other transaction holding that row.

decisions.title: Only a SHA-256 hash of the token is stored
decisions.choice: The `anchor_inv_…` token is returned once, by create and by resend. Lookup and accept hash what they receive and compare hashes.
decisions.why: A database leak does not hand out working invitations. It is the same pattern as API keys.
decisions.instead: Store the token so it can be shown again.
decisions.cost: A lost token cannot be recovered. The Product calls resend, which issues a new token and kills the old one.

decisions.title: Anchor sends no email. The Product delivers the token.
decisions.choice: Anchor owns the invitation record and its lifecycle. Delivery, the email template and the accept page all belong to the Product.
decisions.why: Each Product has its own brand, sender and accept flow. ADR-0019 settles this.
decisions.cost: Every Product has to build its own email and its own accept page.

decisions.title: Accept trusts the token, not the email address
decisions.choice: Accept takes a token and an existing product user. It does not compare the invited email with that user's email, and it never creates a product user.
decisions.why: The Product owns identity. Invitees often sign in with a different address (an alias or SSO).
decisions.instead: Refuse the accept when the emails differ.
decisions.cost: The token works like a password: whoever holds it can join with any product user of that Product.

decisions.title: The token only travels in request bodies
decisions.choice: Lookup and accept are `POST /v1/products/{product_id}/invitations/{lookup,accept}` with the token in the body. An unknown token returns 400, not 404.
decisions.why: URLs end up in access logs, proxies and browser history. The 400 matches the existing rule for identifiers that arrive in a body.
decisions.cost: A read done as a POST: responses cannot be cached, and it is not plain REST.

decisions.title: Accept reuses AddMember in the same transaction
decisions.choice: Accept calls the membership service's `AddMember`, marks the invitation accepted and emits both events inside one transaction.
decisions.why: Membership rules and the `organization.membership.created` event live in one place, so an invited member is exactly like a member added directly.
decisions.instead: Insert the membership row from the invitation service.
decisions.cost: The invitation package now depends on the core service package, and two error constructors there became exported.

ops.note: * 409 if that email already belongs to a member of the organization.

model.hint: Three states. Only accepted is written. Expired happens when the clock passes.

flows.name: Create

steps.t: Generate the token and hash it
No pending invitation for the email
Insert the row with the hash

flows.result: Returns the invitation and the clear token, once.

flows.name: Resend

steps.t: Generate a new token and hash it
Lock the organization, find the invitation
Replace the hash, expiry = now + 7 days

flows.result: The old token stops working. The new one is returned once.

flows.name: Accept
flows.actor: Product, for a signed-in product user · `:update`

steps.t: Hash the token, find the invitation
Read the invitation again under the lock

flows.result: All or nothing. A refused accept emits no event.

flows.name: Lookup

steps.t: Hash the token, find it in this Product
Compute the status from the clock

flows.result: Returns the invitation without the token. It can read expired or accepted.

watch.title: Delete works on accepted and expired invitations
watch.body: Delete has no status check. Deleting an accepted invitation removes its history and emits `organization.invitation.deleted` for something that is already a membership. Is that intended?

watch.title: Resend replaces a custom expiry with the 7-day default
watch.body: Resend sets `expires_at` to now + 7 days. An expiry that was set on create or update is lost.

watch.title: Deleting a role deletes its invitations with no event
watch.body: `product_role_id` cascades. A Product that mirrors invitations from events keeps entries that no longer exist. The PR notes this matches how memberships behave.

watch.title: Existing event endpoints will not receive the new events
watch.body: An endpoint stores an explicit list of event types. Each Product has to add the four invitation types to its endpoint config.

watch.title: `validateStruct` wraps the framework call and adds nothing

apiHint: New permission domain `organization_invitation`. Scopes below drop that prefix.

scenarios.title: Ana gets invited and joins
scenarios.caption: The whole round trip, from an admin clicking Invite to Ana being a member.

steps.label: Invite ana@acme.io as member
steps.say: An admin of Acme invites Ana in the Product UI.

steps.label: POST …/invitations
steps.say: The Product calls Anchor with the email and the role.

steps.label: lock Acme, insert row
steps.say: Anchor locks the organization row, checks the rules, and stores the invitation with only the **hash** of the token.

steps.label: 201 · token anchor_inv_7Hk…
steps.say: The clear token exists in this one response. Anchor cannot show it again.

steps.label: email with accept link
steps.say: The Product sends the email. Anchor sends none.

steps.label: clicks, signs in
steps.say: Ana opens the link and signs in, maybe with a different email address.

steps.label: POST /invitations/lookup {token}
steps.say: The Product looks the token up to render its accept page. The token is in the body, never in the URL.

steps.label: 200 · pending, Acme, member
steps.say: Lookup returns the invitation and its computed status, without the token.

steps.label: POST /invitations/accept {token, user}
steps.say: Ana clicks Accept. The Product sends the token and her existing product user.

steps.label: lock · AddMember · accepted_at
steps.say: One transaction: lock, re-check it is pending, add the membership, mark it accepted.

steps.label: 200 · 2 events emitted
steps.say: `invitation.accepted` and `membership.created` go out together. Ana is a member of Acme.

scenarios.title: Two admins invite Bob at once
scenarios.caption: Why the organization row lock exists. Without it, both requests would see no pending invitation and both would insert.

steps.label: invite bob@acme.io
steps.say: Admin A invites Bob.

steps.label: invite bob@acme.io
steps.say: In the same millisecond, Admin B invites Bob too.

steps.label: SELECT Acme FOR NO KEY UPDATE
steps.say: Request A takes the lock on the Acme row.

steps.label: SELECT Acme FOR NO KEY UPDATE
steps.say: Request B asks for the same lock and **waits**. It has read nothing yet.

steps.label: pending for bob? none
steps.say: Request A checks: no pending invitation for Bob.

steps.label: insert, commit
steps.say: Request A inserts the invitation and commits. The lock is released.

steps.label: 201 created
steps.say: Admin A gets the invitation and its token.

steps.label: lock granted
steps.say: Request B finally gets the lock, and now sees the committed row.

steps.label: pending for bob? yes
steps.say: Request B checks and finds the invitation A just created.

steps.label: 409 ALREADY_PENDING
steps.say: Admin B gets a conflict. Bob has exactly one pending invitation. A CT runs this with eight admins.

scenarios.title: Resend kills the old token
scenarios.caption: Only the hash is stored, so a lost token cannot be shown again. Resend issues a new one and the old one stops working.

steps.label: Ana lost the email, resend
steps.say: Ana deleted the email. The admin clicks Resend.

steps.label: POST …/{id}/resend
steps.say: The Product asks Anchor for a new token.

steps.label: replace hash, expiry = now + 7d
steps.say: Anchor overwrites the hash and resets the expiry. A custom expiry is lost here (see Worth a look).

steps.label: 200 · token anchor_inv_Q2m…
steps.say: The new token is returned once. The Product emails it.

steps.label: accept with anchor_inv_7Hk…
steps.say: Later, someone tries the old link.

steps.label: find by sha256(7Hk…)
steps.say: Anchor hashes the old token and looks it up.

steps.label: no row
steps.say: No row carries that hash any more.

steps.label: 400 TOKEN_NOT_FOUND
steps.say: The old token is refused. Nobody joins.

steps.label: accept with anchor_inv_Q2m…
steps.say: Ana uses the new link.

steps.label: 200 · accepted
steps.say: The new token works. Ana is a member.

schema.hint: One new table, migration 000039. No existing table changes.

organization_invitations.note: An offer to join one organization, sent to one email address, with one role.
notes: No `status` column, no CHECK constraints, no business triggers.
The composite foreign key stops an invitation from pointing at another Product's organization.
The down migration drops the table.

cols.product_id: With `organization_id`, pins the row to its organization's Product
cols.organization_id: Deleting the organization deletes its invitations
cols.email: Stored as given, compared without case
cols.token_hash: SHA-256 of the token. The token itself is never stored.
cols.expires_at: Now + 7 days unless the caller sets it
cols.accepted_at: Set once, on accept. The only stored status signal.

refs.organizations: Row locked by every invitation write

POST /v1/products/{product_id}/organizat.note: Filters by status: pending, accepted, expired
